newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Independent Belgrade radio back on the air.
newsitem.headline: Independent Belgrade radio back on the air.

text.p: An independent Belgrade radio station went back on the air on Thursday after Serbian authorities came under severe international criticism for shutting it down.
A student station, Radio Index, which was also switched off on Tuesday, returned to the air earlier on Thursday.

The small radio stations, together with a handful of independent publications, have offered the only coverage of street demonstrations that erupted after the authorities tried to annul opposition victories in local elections.
The director of state Radio Television Serbia informed B-92 that its transmitter had been knocked out by "heavy rains in the past few days", the state news agency Tanjug reported.
"Radio B-92 is on the air again," staff member Aleksandra Scepanovic said.
State television, radio and newspapers have portrayed the wave of peaceful demonstrations as led by outlaws advocating "terrorism".
Since 1989, Radio B-92 has tried to provide an alternative source of information to the powerful state media.
The last time Serbia was shaken by demonstrations in 1991, President Slobodan Milosevic's police briefly occupied B-92's offices and closed down the station.
Despite repeated requests Radio B-92 still does not have a broadcasting license and staff said they were demanding the authorities grant the necessary documents to resolve the station's legal status.
Radio editors said the authorities still needed to address a fundamental lack of press freedom and democratic rights in Serbia.

"What has happened in recent days in Belgrade has created a new mechanism for a non-violent struggle for freedom of the press and other forms of free speech," Veran Matic, editor-in-chief, told a news conference.
"What is of the utmost importance is that the world started to realise that democracy can be achieved here through the democratisation and liberalisation of the press."
A global network of editors and publishers, the Vienna-based International Press Institute (IPI), condemned the closure of Radio B-92.

The United States condemned the shutdown as "a transparent effort to keep the Serbian public in the dark" and the Voice of America decided to broadcast reports from Radio B-92's correspondents into Serbia.
